narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and worked in your favor, pulling the prediction toward passing. However, your first-year and third-year class rankings were the next two most important factors, and both pushed strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile for both Year 1 and Year 3, well below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These low academic standings in law school outweighed the benefit of your LSAT performance and tipped the overall prediction toward failure.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.3 was also noticeably below the 3.23 average of accepted students, though it had less impact than the three features above. Your family income, full-time status, gender, and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class rank through targeted study and academic support in law school. Retaking the LSAT for a higher score could also help offset weaker rankings. Consider reaching out to the admissions office to discuss specific steps that would strengthen a future application.
